name: Acne Vulgaris (Inflammatory Acne)
description: The skin shows multiple red, inflamed pimples scattered over the cheek area. These are mainly papules (red bumps) and a few pustules (pimples with white centers). This type of acne is commonly caused by excess oil (sebum) production, blocked pores, bacterial growth (Cutibacterium acnes), and hormonal changes (common in teenagers). There are no deep cysts or nodules, which indicates it is not severe acne.
treatment_options: Cleanse face twice daily with a gentle acne cleanser
Apply benzoyl peroxide (2.5%) once daily to reduce bacteria
Use adapalene 0.1% gel at night to prevent new pimples
Use a non-comedogenic moisturizer to avoid dryness
Apply sunscreen (SPF 30+) every morning
home_remedies_supportive: Ice compress (2–3 minutes) to reduce redness
Pure aloe vera gel to soothe inflammation
Green tea compress for mild antibacterial effect
warning: Do NOT pop or squeeze pimples (can cause scars). Avoid harsh scrubs, toothpaste, or lemon on acne. If acne becomes painful, spreads rapidly, or leaves scars, consult a dermatologist. Results take 4–6 weeks — consistency is important.

name: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
description: The skin shows redness, inflammation, dryness, and irritation. The affected area appears sensitive and slightly swollen, which is characteristic of eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition. Eczema commonly occurs due to an overactive immune response, dry or sensitive skin barrier, allergies or irritants (soaps, detergents, dust), and environmental factors (weather changes, pollution). It is non-contagious and may flare up periodically.
treatment_options: Regular use of moisturizers/emollients to restore the skin barrier
Mild topical corticosteroids during flare-ups (as prescribed)
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory creams for long-term management
Gentle skin cleansing with soap-free cleansers
Identification and avoidance of triggers
home_remedies_supportive: Apply thick moisturizers immediately after bathing
Use cold compresses to relieve itching
warning: Avoid scratching, as it can cause skin infections. Do not use strong steroid creams without medical guidance. Long-term neglect may lead to skin thickening or infection. If symptoms worsen, spread rapidly, or show signs of infection, seek medical advice.

name: Psoriasis
description: The skin shows thickened skin with whitish patches and scaling, which is characteristic of psoriasis, a chronic autoimmune skin condition. Psoriasis occurs when skin cells multiply too quickly, leading to thick, scaly plaques, red or inflamed underlying skin, and dryness and surface changes. It is not contagious and often follows a relapsing–remitting pattern, meaning symptoms may improve and flare repeatedly.
treatment_options: Topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation
Vitamin D analog creams to slow skin cell growth
Keratolytic agents (salicylic acid) to reduce scaling
Phototherapy (UV light) in persistent cases
Systemic or biologic therapies for severe disease (doctor-prescribed)
warning: Avoid picking or peeling scales. Do not overuse steroid creams without supervision. Untreated psoriasis may worsen or affect joints (psoriatic arthritis). Seek medical care if lesions spread rapidly, become painful, or crack and bleed.

name: Fungal Skin Infection (Tinea / Ringworm)
description: The rash appears as a round or oval patch with a reddish, raised border and relatively clearer center, which is typical of a fungal skin infection. Fungal infections are caused by dermatophyte fungi that grow on the outer layer of skin. They commonly spread through direct skin-to-skin contact, shared towels/clothes/bedding, and sweating in humid environments. This condition is contagious but usually treatable.
treatment_options: Topical antifungal creams applied 1–2 times daily
Keep the affected area clean and dry
Continue treatment for 1–2 weeks after symptoms improve
In extensive or recurrent cases, oral antifungal medicines may be prescribed by a doctor
home_remedies_supportive: Wash area daily and dry thoroughly
warning: Do NOT use steroid creams alone (can worsen infection). Avoid scratching to prevent spread. Infection may spread to others if untreated. Consult a doctor if there is no improvement in 1–2 weeks or if infection spreads rapidly.

name: Vitiligo
description: The skin shows well-defined light/white patches, which is characteristic of vitiligo, a chronic pigmentary disorder. Vitiligo occurs when melanocytes (pigment-producing cells) are destroyed or stop functioning, leading to loss of skin color. The condition is non-contagious, the skin texture stays normal (no scaling or redness), and it may progress slowly or remain stable over time.
treatment_options: Topical corticosteroids to reduce immune activity
Topical calcineurin inhibitors for long-term control
Phototherapy (UVB light) to stimulate repigmentation
Depigmentation therapy in extensive cases (doctor-guided)
Psychological support for emotional well-being
recommended_products: Camouflage cosmetics to even skin tone
home_remedies_supportive: Use sunscreen daily to prevent contrast darkening
Maintain a balanced diet and manage stress
warning: No guaranteed permanent cure exists. Avoid unproven “miracle” treatments. Sunburn risk is higher on depigmented skin. Consult a dermatologist if patches spread rapidly or affect daily life.

name: Rosacea
description: The skin shows persistent redness with inflamed bumps and visible irritation, which is characteristic of rosacea, a chronic inflammatory skin condition. Rosacea commonly involves facial flushing and redness, small red bumps that may resemble acne, and sensitive, easily irritated skin. Unlike acne, rosacea usually does not involve blackheads and often flares in response to specific triggers.
treatment_options: Topical anti-inflammatory medications (e.g., metronidazole, azelaic acid)
Oral antibiotics for inflammatory flares (doctor-prescribed)
Laser or light therapy for persistent redness
Gentle skincare routine with trigger avoidance
home_remedies_supportive: Identify and avoid triggers (spicy food, heat, sun, alcohol)
Use lukewarm water for face washing
Maintain a simple, fragrance-free skincare routine
warning: Avoid harsh scrubs, exfoliants, or alcohol-based products. Do not self-treat long-term with steroid creams. Untreated rosacea may worsen over time and cause persistent redness. Consult a dermatologist if symptoms become painful, spread rapidly, or affect quality of life.

name: Urticaria (Hives)
description: The skin shows irregular, raised, reddish patches (wheals) that vary in shape and size, typical of urticaria (hives). Hives occur due to release of histamine in the skin, leading to sudden swelling, red or pink patches with clear borders, and intense itching or burning sensation. Urticaria is usually temporary and can appear and disappear within hours.
treatment_options: Oral antihistamines to reduce itching and swelling
Avoid known allergic triggers
Short course of anti-inflammatory medication in severe cases (doctor-prescribed)
Cool environments to reduce flare-ups
home_remedies_supportive: Apply cold compresses to affected areas
warning: Avoid scratching, which can worsen swelling. Do not ignore recurrent or persistent hives. Seek emergency care immediately if hives occur with difficulty breathing, swelling of lips/tongue/throat, dizziness, or fainting. Chronic hives (>6 weeks) require medical evaluation.

name: Impetigo
description: The skin shows red sores with crusting and inflammation, characteristic of impetigo, a common bacterial skin infection. It is usually caused by Staphylococcus or Streptococcus bacteria and is common in children. Key features include red sores that may ooze fluid, formation of yellowish or honey-colored crusts, and easy spread through scratching or close contact. The condition is highly contagious but treatable.
treatment_options: Topical antibiotic ointments for localized infection
Oral antibiotics for widespread or severe cases (doctor-prescribed)
Gentle cleansing of the affected area
Keep nails short to reduce spread
home_remedies_supportive: Clean affected area gently with lukewarm water
warning: Do NOT pick or scratch crusts. Avoid sharing towels, clothes, or toys. Infection can spread quickly if untreated. Seek medical care if fever develops or lesions spread rapidly.

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
description: The skin shows redness with mild inflammation and irritation, typical of seborrheic dermatitis, a chronic inflammatory skin condition. It is associated with overgrowth of Malassezia yeast, increased oil production, and skin sensitivity. It often presents with redness, itching, and flaky or greasy scales and may flare periodically.
treatment_options: Antifungal creams or shampoos to reduce yeast overgrowth
Mild topical corticosteroids for short-term flare control
Anti-inflammatory creams as prescribed
Regular gentle cleansing to control oil buildup
home_remedies_supportive: Wash affected areas regularly with lukewarm water
Avoid harsh soaps and alcohol-based products
warning: Avoid aggressive scrubbing or frequent washing. Do not use strong steroid creams long-term without supervision. Condition may recur. Consult a dermatologist if symptoms worsen, spread, or fail to improve.

name: Normal / Healthy Skin
description: The image shows clear, even-toned skin with no visible inflammation, lesions, redness, scaling, or discoloration. Skin texture appears smooth and balanced, indicating a healthy skin barrier, normal oil and moisture levels, and no signs of infection or chronic skin disease.
treatment_options: No medical treatment required
Maintain a basic skincare routine to preserve skin health
recommended_products: Hydrating face wash suitable for daily use
home_remedies_supportive: Wash face twice daily with lukewarm water
warning: Avoid excessive use of harsh products. Do not over-wash the skin. New symptoms like redness, itching, or lesions should be monitored. Seek medical advice if sudden skin changes occur.
